sections.skill: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths

branch.new_demand: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations preserve the length of a segment.
branch.builds_on: FORWARD 1 applies the definitions in slanted cases; FORWARD 2 uses the same definitions to prove that lengths are kept.

questions.skill: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths
questions.standard_level: Geometry. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Geometry, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.response: write the answer and show the required work
questions.prompt: Points P and Q are on the same side of line ℓ, and line PQ is not perpendicular to ℓ. A reflection across ℓ maps them to P′ and Q′. Let PP′ meet ℓ at M and QQ′ meet ℓ at N. Prove that PQ = P′Q′.
questions.prompt_markup: Points P and Q are on the same side of line ℓ, and line PQ is not perpendicular to ℓ. A reflection across ℓ maps them to P′ and Q′. Let PP′ meet ℓ at M and QQ′ meet ℓ at N. Prove that PQ = P′Q′.
questions.required_method: Use the definition (ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of PP′ and of QQ′), then two pairs of congruent triangles (SAS): PMN ≅ P′MN, then PNQ ≅ P′NQ′.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: PM = P′M and QN = Q′N with right angles at M and N (definition); triangles PMN and P′MN are congruent by SAS, so PN = P′N and ∠PNM ≅ ∠P′NM; subtracting from the right angles gives ∠PNQ ≅ ∠P′NQ′; then triangles PNQ and P′NQ′ are congruent by SAS, so PQ = P′Q′. Alternative: coordinates with ℓ as the x-axis. Invalid: "reflections preserve distance" (that is what is being proved).
